# Value, identity and conversion contracts

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `dotnet-type-semantics` · **C# & .NET Runtime** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q011](#S01-Q011)

<p>Explain value types and reference types through assignment and mutation. How would you predict whether changing one variable affects another?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Predict assignment, conversion and comparison outcomes from an explicit C# type contract.</p>

<ul>
<li>Trace copies, aliases and mutation in value/reference examples.</li>
<li>Distinguish identity, state equality and custom comparison behavior.</li>
<li>Verify type tests and conversions on successful, null and invalid inputs.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>Start by following what each variable contains or refers to. Boxing and casts then change the representation or type view, and equality asks which aspect the application intends to compare; one concrete trace connects these questions.</p>

<a id="S01-Q011"></a>

### S01-Q011 · Foundation

<p>Explain value types and reference types through assignment and mutation. How would you predict whether changing one variable affects another?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q011](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q011)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q011](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q011)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain value types and reference types.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Trace what is copied and what object or value each variable refers to. This asks for semantic behavior before discussing memory layout.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict observable assignment and mutation behavior.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use named C# types, including a reference nested inside a value if helpful; do not infer behavior from stack-versus-heap slogans.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Draws the relationship between variables and state before and after assignment.</li>
<li>Checks a boundary case and explains the assumptions needed for a memory-placement claim.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Reducing the distinction to where memory is stored.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would your prediction change for a struct containing a mutable reference?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q004"></a>

### S01-Q004 · Mechanism

<p>Explain boxing and unboxing using a value passed through object. What must you check before predicting the resulting value or exception?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q004](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q004)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q004](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q004)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain boxing and unboxing.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Trace a conversion step by step rather than memorizing terms. Boxing is the name of a value-type conversion that this example asks you to examine.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict conversion behavior from declared and actual types.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a small C# value-type example; keep numeric conversion, object identity and nullable input assumptions explicit.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Tracks types and values across the conversion and a failed attempt.</li>
<li>Uses a runnable example before drawing allocation or hot-path conclusions.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating an unboxing operation as an arbitrary numeric conversion.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you investigate repeated conversions in a performance-sensitive loop?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q020"></a>

### S01-Q020 · Mechanism

<p>What does equality mean for the value and reference types in your example? Distinguish equal state from referring to the same object.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q020](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q020)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q020](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q020)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain equality semantics for value and reference types.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Define the application’s meaning of equality, then examine the type’s default or customized behavior. This question focuses on type semantics, not just choosing an operator.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain and verify an equality contract for concrete types.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the types and any custom equality or hashing; do not assume all value types or all reference types share one behavior.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Separates state equality, identity and the method used to compare them.</li>
<li>Tests equal and unequal inputs and checks consistency when the type is used as a key.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Equating every reference-type comparison with object identity.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What can go wrong if a key’s equality-relevant state changes after insertion?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q005"></a>

### S01-Q005 · Application

<p>When can == and Equals() give different results in C#? Show how you would determine the intended comparison for a particular type.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q005](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q005)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q005](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q005)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What is the difference between `==` and `Equals()`?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>The question contrasts an operator with a method call. Explain how declared types and the type’s equality contract affect your prediction.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Select and defend a comparison operation for an explicit input contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the concrete type, possible nulls and any overloaded operator or overridden equality method; do not generalize from strings alone.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Predicts results for a representative type and checks null boundaries.</li>
<li>Explains how the chosen comparison relates to the application’s meaning of equal.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming one operation always compares values and the other always compares references.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you test a custom type whose equality implementation is changed?</li>
</ul>

</details>

**What to clarify**

<p>Compare a type test with a conversion attempt and explain how the surrounding code handles the outcome. Keep the required output contract clear.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Handle uncertain input types without hiding invalid assumptions.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the C# version and exact syntax; consult official documentation for pattern forms or type restrictions being used.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Predicts successful, unsuccessful and null cases for the chosen types.</li>
<li>Explains how the caller distinguishes an accepted input from an invalid one.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming every form of type checking and casting has the same supported types or failure behavior.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What changes when the accepted input is a value type rather than a reference type?</li>
</ul>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical component receives objects, recognizes a supported type and stores accepted values in a keyed collection. Predict assignment and mutation effects, a valid and invalid conversion, and equality for two separately constructed inputs. Specify the contract and write checks before discussing resource costs.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Predicts basic assignment, conversion and comparison for named types.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends null and invalid-type handling and tests equality consistency at the collection boundary.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>Stack/heap slogans or a successful cast alone do not demonstrate the complete input contract.</p>
